“There is no doubt,” K. said very quietly, pleased by the strained attention of the entire gathering; in this silence there arose a rushing sound more stirring than the most ecstatic applause, “there is no doubt that behind every manifestation of this court—in my case, then, behind the arrest and today's examination—stands a large organisation. An organisation that employs not only corruptible guards, foolish supervisors and examining magistrates who are mediocre at best, but also, certainly, maintains a judiciary of high and the highest ranks, with the countless, indispensable retinue of attendants, clerks, gendarmes and other assistants, perhaps even executioners—I don't shrink from the word. And the purpose of this large organisation, gentlemen? It consists in arresting innocent people and instituting senseless proceedings against them, usually, as in my case, without result. Given the senselessness of the whole thing, how could the worst corruption among the officials be concealed? It's impossible; even the highest judge could not manage that for himself alone. That is why the guards try to steal the clothes off arrested people's backs, why supervisors break into other people's homes, why the innocent are to be humiliated before entire gatherings rather than questioned. The guards merely told me about storerooms where the arrested people's property is taken. I'd like to see those storage places, where the possessions they have worked so hard to acquire are rotting, insofar as they haven't been stolen by thieving storeroom officials.”

K. was interrupted by a shriek from the far end of the hall. He shaded his eyes to see, because the dull daylight made the haze whitish and dazzling. It concerned the washerwoman, whom K. had recognised as a serious disturbance as soon as she entered. Whether she was now at fault or not could not be made out. K. saw only that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was pressing her against him there. But it was not she who was shrieking; it was the man. His mouth was stretched wide and he was looking at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around them; the people in the nearby gallery seemed delighted that the seriousness K. had introduced into the gathering had been interrupted in this way. His first impulse was to run over at once. He also thought everyone would want order restored there, and at least the couple removed from the hall, but the first rows in front of him remained solid; no one moved and no one let K. through. On the contrary, they obstructed him, and a hand—he had no time to turn round—seized him from behind by the collar. Old men held out their arms. K. was no longer really thinking of the couple; he felt as though his freedom were being restricted, as though they were making the arrest a serious matter, and he jumped down from the platform without regard for anyone. Now he stood eye to eye with the crowd. Had he misjudged these people? Had he expected too much effect from his speech? Had they been pretending while he spoke, and now that he was coming to his conclusions, were they tired of pretending? What faces surrounded him! Small black eyes darted back and forth; cheeks sagged like drunkards'; the long beards were stiff and sparse, and when hands reached into them, it seemed as though people were merely forming claws rather than grasping beards. But beneath the beards—and this was K.'s real discovery—badges of various sizes and colours gleamed on the coat collars. Everyone had these badges, as far as he could see. They all belonged together, the apparent parties on the right and left; and when he turned suddenly, he saw the same badges on the collar of the examining magistrate, who was looking calmly down with his hands in his lap. “So!” cried K., throwing his arms up; the sudden realisation demanded space. “You're all officials, I see. You're the corrupt gang I was speaking against. You've crowded in here as listeners and snoopers, pretended to form parties, and one of them applauded to test me. You wanted to learn how to lead innocent people astray. Well, I hope you've truly been here for nothing. Either you've amused yourselves at someone expecting you to defend innocence, or else—let go of me or I'll hit you!” K. shouted at a trembling old man who had pushed particularly close to him—“or else you've really learnt something. And with that I wish you luck in your trade.” He quickly took his hat, which lay on the edge of the table, and pushed towards the exit amid general silence, certainly the silence of utter surprise. But the examining magistrate seemed to have been even quicker than K., for he was waiting for him by the door. “One moment,” he said. K. stopped, but looked not at the examining magistrate, only at the door, whose handle he had already grasped. “I merely wanted to point out,” said the examining magistrate, “that today—you probably haven't realised it yet—you have deprived yourself of the advantage that questioning offers an arrested person in every case.” K. laughed at the door. “You scoundrels, you can keep all your questioning!” he shouted, opening the door and hurrying down the stairs. Behind him rose the noise of the gathering, lively once more, beginning to discuss the incidents in the manner of students.
